result: The study recruited eight neurologically healthy volunteers (six male, aged 28.5 ± 8.52 years) who completed 1-5 sessions on different days, resulting in 540-2700 trials per participant (M = 1822.5, SD = 813.21). The study protocol was approved by the UCL Research Ethics Committee (reference number 5833/001). In most trials (70%), the direction of coherent motion in the RDK was congruent to the direction of the instruction cue.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C3, and C38 provide explicit methodological details about participant recruitment, ethics approval, experimental design, and data collection. These are straightforward descriptive claims that are well-documented in the manuscript.

result: Behavioral performance showed that accuracy increased with increasing coherence in congruent trials, with a significant interaction between congruence and coherence for accuracy (χ²(2) = 363.21, p<0.001). Response times were faster during congruent trials than incongruent trials at all coherence levels, with significant pairwise comparisons at low, medium, and high coherence levels (all p<0.001).
evaluation: Claims C4, C5, and C6 present behavioral results with appropriate statistical tests (generalized linear mixed model for accuracy, linear mixed model for RT, and Tukey-corrected pairwise comparisons). The statistical analyses are appropriate for the data type and the results are clearly reported with effect sizes and significance levels.

result: The head-cast technology achieved high spatial precision with within-session movement <0.2 mm in x and y dimensions and <1.5 mm in z dimension, and co-registration error <1.5 mm in any dimension. Data reproducibility was excellent, with ICC greater than 0.9 for all task epochs for the example participant and mean ICC greater than 0.85 across all subjects for all task epochs and reproducibility measures.
evaluation: Claims C7-C10 document the technical performance of the head-cast technology with quantitative metrics. The ICC values demonstrate excellent test-retest reliability, which is critical for the laminar discrimination analyses. These measurements are well-documented with supporting figures.

result: Visual cortex showed expected task-related spectral changes, with significant decreases in alpha (7-13 Hz) and increases in gamma (60-90 Hz) power following RDK onset, consistent with prior literature on attention to visual stimuli. Additionally, a burst of gamma activity was observed following the instruction cue onset.
evaluation: Claims C11-C13 describe well-established patterns of visual cortical activity that were replicated in this study. The findings are supported by sensor-level analyses with appropriate statistical corrections (p<0.05, Bonferroni corrected) and are consistent with cited prior work.

result: Sensorimotor cortex exhibited characteristic movement-related spectral patterns, including a decrease in beta power (15-30 Hz) prior to and during the response with subsequent rebound, and a burst of response-aligned gamma (60-90 Hz) activity. These patterns are consistent with established literature on motor-related brain activity.
evaluation: Claims C14-C17 describe well-characterized sensorimotor activity patterns that were successfully replicated at the sensor level. The findings are supported by appropriate statistical analyses (p<0.05, Bonferroni corrected) and align with extensive prior literature on motor cortex activity.

result: Visual alpha activity (7-13 Hz) predominantly originated from deep cortical laminae (white matter surface), while visual gamma activity (60-90 Hz) originated from more superficial laminae (pial surface) in both RDK-aligned and instruction cue-aligned epochs. This laminar dissociation was statistically significant across multiple ROI definitions (global, functional, and anatomical).
evaluation: Claims C18-C21, C67-C68 present the core finding for visual cortex laminar organization. The results are supported by rigorous statistical analyses using Wilcoxon tests across multiple ROI definitions, with consistent findings showing visual alpha localizing to white matter surface (8/8 participants globally) and gamma to pial surface (7/8 participants). The findings are consistent with invasive recordings in non-human primates.

result: Sensorimotor beta activity (both pre-movement decrease and post-movement rebound) localized to deep cortical laminae (white matter surface), while movement-related gamma activity localized to superficial laminae (pial surface). This laminar specificity in sensorimotor cortex echoed the pattern observed in visual cortex.
evaluation: Claims C22-C24, C69 demonstrate that the laminar organization principle extends to sensorimotor cortex. Statistical support is strong with Wilcoxon tests showing beta localizing to white matter surface (global: W(8)=0, p=0.008 for decrease; W(8)=1, p=0.016 for rebound) and gamma to pial surface (global: W(8)=35, p=0.016, 7/8 participants). This represents the first non-invasive evidence for laminar organization in human sensorimotor cortex.

result: Control analyses demonstrated that laminar discrimination depends on precise anatomical models and is not simply driven by lead field strength differences. Shuffling sensor positions resulted in all signals localizing to the pial surface, while the relationship between lead field strength and laminar preference was not frequency-specific. When vertices were matched for lead field strength, low frequency signals still localized to deep layers.
evaluation: Claims C25, C47-C49 describe critical control analyses that validate the main findings. The sensor shuffling control (Figure 5-supplement 1) demonstrates that the laminar effects depend on accurate spatial information. The lead field analyses (Figure 5-supplements 6-7) show that while there is a correlation between lead field strength and laminar preference, this relationship is constant across frequencies and the laminar dissociation persists when controlling for lead field strength.

result: Visual gamma activity on the pial surface following instruction cue onset was significantly greater in incongruent compared to congruent trials (W(8)=0, p=0.008; 8/8 participants; M difference = 1.64%, SD = 2.34%). This enhancement is consistent with gamma activity increases observed during perceptual expectation violations.
evaluation: Claims C26, C50, C60 demonstrate that superficial visual gamma activity is modulated by task demands in a theoretically predicted manner. The statistical evidence is strong (all 8 participants showed the effect) and the interpretation aligns with cited literature on prediction error processing. This provides functional validation of the laminar localization.

result: Deep sensorimotor beta activity showed task-dependent modulation: the pre-movement beta decrease was more pronounced with increasing RDK coherence (X²(2)=9.75, p=0.008), and the post-movement beta rebound was greater in congruent compared to incongruent trials (W(8)=34, p=0.023; 7/8 participants; M difference = 5.13%, SD = 5.19%).
evaluation: Claims C27-C28, C51-C52 demonstrate that deep layer sensorimotor beta activity is functionally relevant to motor preparation and performance monitoring. The statistical evidence is robust with appropriate tests (Friedman test for coherence effect, Wilcoxon test for congruence effect). These findings provide functional validation of the laminar localization and suggest complex roles for beta activity beyond simple feedback signaling.

result: The study was motivated by theoretical proposals that the cerebral cortex is hierarchically organized via feedback and feedforward connections originating from deep and superficial layers, respectively, with lower frequency activity (<40 Hz) subserving feedback communication via infragranular layers and higher frequency activity (>40 Hz) conveying feedforward information via supragranular layers.
evaluation: Claims C29-C33, C65-C66 accurately describe the theoretical framework and prior evidence from animal studies that motivated the current work. These claims are well-supported by extensive citations to anatomical and electrophysiological literature. The authors appropriately distinguish between established anatomical principles and theoretical proposals about functional roles.

result: MEG is a direct measure of neural activity with millisecond temporal precision. The 3D printed head-cast technology provides enhanced stability in head positioning and precise anatomical models, allowing recording of higher SNR MEG data than previously achievable. Theoretical and simulation work demonstrates that these gains allow, in principle, for distinguishing MEG signals originating from deep versus superficial laminae.
evaluation: Claims C34-C37 describe the methodological foundation of the study with appropriate citations. The claims about MEG capabilities and head-cast advantages are supported by prior published work. The statement about theoretical feasibility is appropriately qualified ('in principle') and cites relevant simulation studies.

result: The study employed high-resolution (800 μm isotropic) MRI multi-parameter maps for cortical surface extraction, 275-channel CTF MEG system with 1200 Hz sampling rate, and empirical Bayesian beamformer (EBB) for source reconstruction. Data preprocessing included filtering (2-100 Hz bandpass, 50 Hz notch), downsampling to 250 Hz, and eye-blink artifact removal. All data are archived at the Open MEG Archive.
evaluation: Claims C39-C46 provide comprehensive methodological details about data acquisition and preprocessing. These are explicit, verifiable statements about equipment, parameters, and procedures. The high-resolution MRI is particularly important for accurate laminar discrimination, as discussed in the manuscript.

result: The localization of alpha activity to deep laminae and gamma activity to superficial laminae in visual cortex is consistent with invasive depth electrode recordings in non-human primates. The superficial origin of gamma is supported by the anatomical distribution of local recurrent connections and fast-spiking interneurons, which are most numerous in supragranular layers.
evaluation: Claims C53-C56 appropriately contextualize the current findings within prior invasive recording literature and known anatomical principles. The comparisons are well-supported by citations and the authors appropriately note some conflicting evidence (e.g., Nandy et al., 2017). The mechanistic explanations for gamma generation are consistent with established neuroscience.

result: The sensorimotor findings are consistent with in vitro recordings showing beta activity generated in circuits dominated by infragranular layer V pyramidal cells and gamma arising from supragranular layers II/III. The results provide the first non-invasive evidence for the laminar origin of movement-related sensorimotor activity.
evaluation: Claims C57-C59 appropriately contextualize the sensorimotor findings. The authors correctly note the lack of in vivo laminar data from primate sensorimotor cortex and cite relevant in vitro studies. The claim of novelty (C59) is justified given the lack of prior non-invasive human evidence for laminar organization in sensorimotor cortex.

result: The dissociation between bottom-up and top-down influences during different task epochs suggests that sensorimotor beta decrease and rebound may result from functionally distinct processes. The findings suggest that distinct frequency channels operate in a lamina-specific manner across cortex but may fulfill distinct functional roles in sensory versus motor processes, representing a more complex organization than simple feedback/feedforward communication.
evaluation: Claims C61, C70-C71 present interpretations and speculations about the functional significance of the findings. While the laminar localization data are solid, the functional interpretations are necessarily speculative because the study did not directly assess inter-regional communication or test specific predictions about feedback/feedforward processing. The authors appropriately use cautious language ('could indicate', 'may fulfill', 'suggest') but these remain hypotheses requiring further testing.

result: The ROI-based comparison can only determine the origin of the strongest source of activity and does not imply exclusive confinement to one lamina. Future work with wearable MEG sensors (optically pumped magnetometers) that do not require cryogenic cooling and can be placed directly on the scalp surface promises to extend the reach of laminar MEG by directly increasing SNR.
evaluation: Claims C62-C64 appropriately acknowledge limitations of the current approach and discuss future directions. C62 correctly notes that the binary comparison (deep vs. superficial) identifies the dominant source but does not exclude activity in other layers. C63-C64 accurately describe emerging technology with appropriate citations, though the promise of this technology remains to be fully demonstrated.
